Healthy.label: Healthy
Healthy.description: Leaf exhibits no apparent signs of disease in the image. Regular monitoring is still recommended as early-stage symptoms may not yet be prominently visible on foliage.
symptoms: Uniform green leaf blade with consistent texture.
Absence of necrotic lesions, brown spots, white powdery patches, serpentine mines, or abnormal yellow halos.
No visible damage from foliar epidermal chewing or sucking pests.
causes: No visible pathogen or pest infestation detected in the input image.
Minor mechanical abrasions or slight physiological yellowing do not indicate infectious disease.
treatments: Maintain current agricultural care and management practices.
Re-inspect in 3-5 days if neighboring field areas show disease foci.
Do not apply chemical pesticides based solely on a healthy diagnosis if distinct field symptoms appear.
prevention: Maintain field and orchard sanitation; promptly remove fallen diseased foliage and plant debris.
Apply balanced fertilization, avoiding excessive nitrogen that predisposes plants to infections.
Regularly inspect leaf undersides and older canopy layers for early signs of pests or pathogens.

BrownSpot.label: BrownSpot
BrownSpot.description: Brown spot on rice typically produces circular or oval brown lesions on the leaf surface. Disease severity increases under nutritional deficiencies, physiological stress, or unbalanced soil conditions.
symptoms: Small, circular to oval brown spots across the leaf blade.
Lesion centers may turn light grayish-white with distinct dark brown margins.
In severe infections, lesions coalesce to form extensive blighted areas across the leaf.
causes: Fungal pathogen (Bipolaris oryzae) overwintering on infected seeds, crop residue, or volunteer hosts.
Potassium and silicon deficiencies, nutrient-depleted soils, or impaired root systems.
High relative humidity, prolonged leaf wetness, and poor water management accelerating infection.
treatments: Incorporate or remove infected crop residue post-harvest to reduce primary inoculum.
Adjust fertilizer regime, supplementing potassium, silicon, and lime based on local soil tests.
Maintain consistent irrigation and drainage to alleviate prolonged crop stress.
If infection spreads rapidly, consult plant protection specialists to select authorized fungicides.
prevention: Use certified, pathogen-free seed and disease-tolerant cultivars.
Sow at recommended spacing to promote adequate canopy ventilation.
Apply balanced fertilizers with split nitrogen applications to prevent lush growth.
Closely monitor fields with a history of brown spot during early tillering.

sources.title: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank - rice disease resources

LeafBlast.label: LeafBlast
LeafBlast.description: Rice leaf blast is a major destructive disease characterized by spindle- or eye-shaped lesions with grayish centers. The disease flourishes in cool, humid weather accompanied by excessive nitrogen application.
symptoms: Spindle-shaped (elliptical) lesions with grayish-white centers and dark brown margins.
Rapid coalescence of lesions resulting in complete foliar blight and leaf death.
Severe infection stunts tillering, weakens plant vigor, and substantially reduces yield.
causes: Magnaporthe oryzae fungus thriving under high humidity (>90%), heavy dew, and prolonged fog or rain.
Excessive nitrogen fertilizer promoting lush, succulent foliar tissue with thin epidermal walls.
Inoculum reservoirs residing on infected straw, stubble, ratoons, and adjacent fields.
treatments: Immediately halt additional nitrogen fertilizer applications when symptoms spread.
Promote canopy aeration and maintain stable water depth to minimize plant stress.
Eliminate inoculum sources by roguing infected ratoon rice and clearing field borders.
Consult local plant protection specialists immediately for targeted fungicide interventions before panicle initiation.
prevention: Cultivate blast-resistant rice varieties adapted to the agro-ecological region.
Adhere to optimal sowing density, avoiding overly dense canopies.
Apply balanced NPK fertilization with split nitrogen dosages matched to growth stages.
Monitor fields vigilantly during cool, damp weather, extended overcast periods, or after prolonged rainfall.

Hispa.label: Hispa
Hispa.description: Rice hispa is a foliar insect pest. Both adult beetles and leaf-mining grubs scrape leaf epidermis and tunnel through mesophyll, creating distinctive white streaks and reducing photosynthetic area.
symptoms: Parallel white or silvery streaks along the leaf veins.
Scraped epidermal tissue resembling narrow withered stripes.
In dense infestations, foliage turns entirely white, withers, and severely curtails plant growth.
causes: Adult beetles feeding on upper epidermis while grubs mine inside the leaf parenchyma.
Overly dense crop stands, abundant grassy weeds, and close planting providing sheltered microclimates.
Favorable weather conditions and infested neighboring fields causing rapid population surges.
treatments: Assess hispa population density across multiple field sampling points before taking action.
Thin out excessively dense patches to enhance sunlight penetration and aeration.
Clear weed vegetation along bunds and eliminate ratoon rice to destroy alternate hosts.
Preserve natural predators; apply registered insecticides only when economic injury thresholds are exceeded.
prevention: Synchronize community planting schedules to disrupt continuous hispa migration cycles.
Maintain weed-free levees, bunds, and irrigation channels.
Scout young leaves and fields near infested zones following rain or humid spells.
Avoid indiscriminate broad-spectrum sprays that decimate beneficial natural enemy populations.

LeafMiner.label: LeafMiner
LeafMiner.name_vi: Sâu vẽ bùa hại lá cà phê
LeafMiner.description: Coffee leaf miner larvae feed within the leaf mesophyll, creating characteristic serpentine mines or necrotic blotches. Severe infestations impair photosynthesis and induce premature leaf abscission.
symptoms: Serpentine white or translucent mines and dry blistered patches across the leaf surface.
Mined areas turn yellowish-brown and eventually become brittle and necrotic.
Premature defoliation, particularly on older foliage and severely damaged branches.
causes: Larvae of Leucoptera coffeella feeding exclusively on inner leaf parenchyma.
Hot, dry microclimates, water-stressed trees, and sparse shade cover favoring rapid insect reproduction.
Disruption of parasitoid wasps and predator populations due to improper chemical applications.
treatments: Collect and destroy heavily mined fallen leaves under the tree canopy to reduce pupal emergence.
Prune trees to establish a well-aerated canopy while preserving balanced shade cover.
Assess leaf infestation percentage before initiating management interventions.
Conserve natural parasitoids; apply selective, approved bio-rational insecticides if damage thresholds are breached.
prevention: Maintain tree vigor through balanced irrigation, mulching, and soil fertilization.
Avoid broad-spectrum chemical sprays when pest populations are below economic thresholds.
Routinely inspect mature leaves during the onset of dry periods.
Manage understory weeds and fallen leaf litter beneath the tree canopy.

PowderyMildew.label: PowderyMildew
PowderyMildew.name_vi: Bệnh phấn trắng trên cà phê
PowderyMildew.description: Powdery mildew produces a white, powdery fungal coating over leaves, shoots, and young buds. The disease is favored by high relative humidity, poor canopy airflow, and shaded conditions.
symptoms: Superficial white powdery patches on the upper leaf surface, young twigs, or shoots.
Curling, chlorosis, and distortion of young, developing foliage.
Heavily infected tissue undergoes necrosis, turns dull brown, and withers.
causes: Erysiphales fungi proliferating in humid, warm conditions with poor air circulation.
Dense, unpruned canopies, inadequate sunlight penetration, or excessive nitrogen fertilization.
Airborne conidia dispersing readily across foliage via light breezes and mechanical contact.
treatments: Prune severely affected shoots and foliage, discarding them away from the orchard.
Open the canopy through corrective pruning to enhance light penetration and reduce humidity.
Regulate irrigation schedules to avoid prolonged moisture accumulation on leaves.
When infection accelerates, consult plant health specialists to apply approved sulfur or bio-fungicide treatments.
prevention: Perform routine pruning to ensure optimal air circulation throughout the tree canopy.
Apply balanced fertilizers, avoiding excess nitrogen that induces lush, susceptible growth.
Inspect coffee trees closely after persistent overcast, foggy, or damp weather.
Keep the ground free of dense weed cover and rotting plant residues.

Rust.label: Rust
Rust.description: Coffee leaf rust is a devastating fungal disease identified by yellow-orange powdery pustules on the lower leaf surface. Severe infection causes massive defoliation, branch dieback, and sharp yield losses.
symptoms: Bright yellow to orange powdery pustules (uredinia) on the underside of leaves.
Chlorotic yellow spots on the upper leaf surface corresponding to pustules below.
Diseased leaves turn necrotic, dry out, and drop prematurely, causing canopy defoliation.
causes: Hemileia vastatrix fungus dispersing urediniospores primarily via wind, rain splash, and contact.
High humidity, prolonged leaf wetness (>24 hours), and dense tree canopies accelerating spore germination.
Nutrient depletion or high crop bearing load increasing physiological vulnerability to infection.
treatments: Rake and compost or bury heavily infected fallen leaves to diminish the spore reservoir.
Selectively prune to enhance ventilation and accelerate canopy drying after rain.
Apply post-infection restorative nutrition to aid tree recovery.
Contact extension officers or agricultural authorities for timely application of protective copper or systemic fungicides.
prevention: Plant rust-resistant coffee cultivars suitable for local elevation and climate.
Manage shade trees to provide balanced light, avoiding continuous high humidity.
Routinely inspect leaf undersides starting at the onset of the rainy season.
Prevent post-harvest exhaustion by maintaining adequate soil nutrient replenishment.

AlgalLeafSpot.label: AlgalLeafSpot
AlgalLeafSpot.name_vi: Bệnh đốm rong trên cà phê
AlgalLeafSpot.description: Algal leaf spot (green scurf) produces slightly raised, velvety circular lesions with grayish-green to rust-brown coloration. It occurs primarily in damp, shaded orchards on weakened coffee trees.
symptoms: Circular or subcircular, slightly raised spots on the leaf surface.
Lesion color transitioning from grayish-green to velvety yellowish-brown or rust-red.
Coalescing lesions reduce photosynthetic efficiency and may trigger premature yellowing and leaf drop.
causes: Parasitic green alga (Cephaleuros virescens) thriving in warm, damp, poorly ventilated environments.
Overly dense canopies, waterlogged soil, poor air movement, and general tree debility.
Rain splash and continuous high moisture aiding the spread of zoospores across foliage.
treatments: Prune inner branches to open the canopy and decrease ambient relative humidity.
Remove heavily infested leaves and improve soil drainage around tree basins.
Apply balanced fertilization to restore tree vigor and leaf resilience.
If defoliation occurs, consult plant protection advisors regarding targeted copper-based treatments.
prevention: Maintain proper planting distances and canopy pruning schedules.
Control dense weed growth and wet organic matter accumulation beneath the canopy.
Scout for early lesion development following prolonged monsoon or rainy periods.
Avoid excessively dense overhead shade trees that restrict sunlight and airflow.
